THOUGHT: This 50-year-old male presents with subacute onset (2 months) of chronic cough, systemic symptoms (fever, malaise, elevated ESR), and musculoskeletal complaints (aching hips and lower back). His travel history to Phoenix, Arizona — an endemic area for *Coccidioides* species — is highly relevant. The chest imaging shows right middle lobe consolidation, small pleural effusion, and hilar adenopathy — findings consistent with pulmonary coccidioidomycosis. Critically, the lung biopsy reveals necrotizing granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells and spherules containing endospores — the pathognomonic histopathologic hallmark of *Coccidioides immitis/posadasii*. The PAS and silver methenamine stains are positive (highlighting fungal elements), while acid-fast stain is negative — effectively ruling out mycobacterial infection (e.g., TB). The absence of weight loss, night sweats, and international travel makes malignancy or disseminated TB less likely. Although he has hypertension, clopamide (a thiazide diuretic) is not immunosuppressive; however, even immunocompetent individuals can develop symptomatic or disseminated coccidioidomycosis, especially after significant environmental exposure. The joint pain and lower back tenderness may reflect hematogenous dissemination — a known complication of coccidioidomycosis (“Valley Fever”) — including osteomyelitis or reactive arthropathy (e.g., erythema nodosum or polyarthralgia, though here it’s more suggestive of bony involvement given location and chronicity). The fever (38.6°C), tachycardia, and elevated ESR further support active systemic fungal infection. All evidence converges on primary pulmonary coccidioidomycosis with possible early dissemination.

DIAGNOSIS: Coccidioidomycosis
